title: Starbucks and the Habit of Success
coreMove: Rehearse the first response to a stressful cue before self-control has to improvise.
sourcePressure: Starbucks training routines show willpower becoming automatic through scripts, scenarios, and stress planning. The chapter does not praise politeness or grit in the abstract; it shows how practiced responses change what happens when pressure hits.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version tells readers to be resilient or stay calm with customers. The writer must show a concrete script practiced before the cue, so self-control is a routine rather than a trait.

hook: A barista smiles through a rude customer.
A person discovers they simply need more grit.
counterintuition: Most people think willpower is a trait, but actually...
Treating stress planning as a motivational mantra.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and breathe.
Promise to stay calm next time.
Write a vague if-then plan without speaking the first line.
examples: Seafood line-cook anger substitution from ch03.
Crisis redesign instead of rehearsed first response.

exampleSpecs.audience: a seasonal bookseller who freezes when a customer slams a gift receipt on the counter
exampleSpecs.stakes: one defensive reply can turn a solvable return into a public argument in a packed store
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before opening, the manager has the bookseller practice the first sentence with a bent gift receipt in hand; when the receipt hits the counter later, the practiced line comes out before the old flinch.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A bent gift receipt lies under a stack of returned hardcovers.

exampleSpecs.domain: medical imaging front desk running two hours behind
exampleSpecs.audience: a receptionist who gets rattled when anxious patients demand exact wait times
exampleSpecs.stakes: a bad first response can make a frightened patient leave before a needed scan
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The supervisor rehearses the exact opening line beside the delay board; when a patient points at the clock and raises his voice, the receptionist reads the first sentence from memory and then checks the scanner queue.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A delay board shows two hours beside a quiet MRI hallway.

exampleSpecs.domain: youth hockey referee facing a parent protest
exampleSpecs.audience: a new referee who loses control when adults crowd the glass after a penalty
exampleSpecs.stakes: one shouted answer can turn a youth game into a bench-clearing mess
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The referee trainer predicts the shove at the glass will be the cue, then drills whistle, two steps back, and the same penalty explanation until the sequence appears during the actual protest.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A black puck sits still near a scuffed penalty-box door.

exampleSpecs.domain: free tax-prep clinic when a refund is smaller than expected
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer preparer who tends to overexplain when clients get angry
exampleSpecs.stakes: a confusing answer can make a low-income client mistrust the whole filing and walk out without submitting
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The clinic lead chooses role-play over another tax-law handout; the volunteer practices pointing to the refund line, naming the change, and pausing before explanation so the first response is ready when the chair scrapes back.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A refund line glows on a laptop beside a half-zipped folder.

exampleSpecs.domain: concert hall usher refusing re-entry during a live recording
exampleSpecs.audience: an usher who caves when late patrons insist they only need ten seconds
exampleSpecs.stakes: one opened door can ruin the recording take and anger the people already seated
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before rehearsal, the usher argues and apologizes; after three practiced doorway scripts with the house manager, she holds the velvet rope and gives the same first line when a patron reaches for the handle.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A velvet rope cuts across a dim concert-hall doorway.
mustAvoid: film festival volunteer lanyard from ch02

exampleSpecs.audience: a clerk who gets defensive when travelers blame her for an impossible same-day request
exampleSpecs.stakes: one irritated exchange can shut down the only path to a workable appointment
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After reviewing the complaint log, the supervisor marks the cue as a traveler tapping the appointment slip and drills the clerk's first two sentences until the next tap triggers the script instead of a snapped answer.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An appointment slip is tapped against a scratched service window.

skillTargets: identify the stressful cue that needs a rehearsed first response
choose scripts that are practiced before pressure instead of invented during pressure
distinguish trained willpower routines from vague calm-down advice or personality praise
evaluate whether a scenario plan includes enough rehearsal to change the default response

tryThisNowSpec: Choose one stressful cue you can predict. Write the first sentence you want available, say it out loud twice, then place the cue word beside it so the line is tied to the moment.
